--- knitr: opts_chunk: comment: "" --- # Reference Semantics {#sec-dtrefsem} This chapter introduces the concept of [reference semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_strategy#Call_by_reference), which is used by the `data.table` package.

When you create an object in R, it is stored at some location in memory. The `address()` function in the `data.table` package returns the memory address of an object. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(data.table) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'data.table' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following object is masked from 'package:base': %notin% ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} options(datatable.print.class = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Add column to data.frame Let's create a simple data.frame, `df1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df1 <- data.frame( ID = c(8001, 8002), GCS = c(15, 13) ) ``` ::: ...and print its address: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e91d1688" ``` ::: ::: Right now, we don't care what the actual address is - but we want to keep track when it changes. Let's add a new column to `df1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df1[["HR"]] <- c(80, 90) ``` ::: ...and print its address: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e9b0de08" ``` ::: ::: The address has changed, even though we're still working on the "same" `df1` object. ## Add column to data.table Let's create a simple data.table, `dt1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1 <- data.table( ID = c(8001, 8002), GCS = c(15, 13) ) ``` ::: ...and print its address: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e7cea000" ``` ::: ::: Let's add a new column to `dt1` ***in-place***: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1[, HR := c(80, 90)] ``` ::: ...and print its address: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e7cea000" ``` ::: ::: The address remains the same. What if we had used the data.frame syntax (which still works on a data.table) instead? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1[["HR_too"]] <- c(80, 90) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e8253098" ``` ::: ::: The address indeed changes, just like with data.frames. ::: callout-important Making copies of large objects can be time-consuming and memory-intensive. Up to this point, we have seen that making changes to data.table by reference, changes the object in-place and does not create a new copy. ::: ## Caution with reference semantics So far so good, we start to understand one reason why `data.table` is efficient. One very important thing to keep in mind is that when you do want to make a copy of a data.table, e.g. to create a different version of it, you must use `data.tables`'s `copy()`. Let's see why. ### Copying a data.frame Let's remind ourselves of the contents and address of `df1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR 1 8001 15 80 2 8002 13 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e9b0de08" ``` ::: ::: To make a copy of `df1`, we can simply assign it to a new object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df2 <- df1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR 1 8001 15 80 2 8002 13 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e9b0de08" ``` ::: ::: The address of `df2` is the same as `df1`, which means they are pointing to the same object in memory. As we've already seen, if we edit `df2`, its address will change: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df2[1, 3] <- 75 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR 1 8001 15 75 2 8002 13 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e98f2be8" ``` ::: ::: The contents and address of `df2` have changed, but `df1` remains the same, as you might expect: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR 1 8001 15 80 2 8002 13 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(df1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e9b0de08" ``` ::: ::: ### Copying a data.table Let's remind ourselves of the contents and address of `dt1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 80 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e8253098" ``` ::: ::: Let's see what happens if we assign `dt1` to a new object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt2 <- dt1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 80 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e8253098" ``` ::: ::: So far it's the same as with data.frames. Let's see what happens if we edit `dt2` by reference: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt2[1, HR := 75] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 75 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e8253098" ``` ::: ::: and let's recheck `dt1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 75 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: `dt1` has changed as well, because `dt1` and `dt2` are still pointing to the same object in memory! This is crucial to remember to avoid errors and confusion. ::: callout-important When you want to make a copy of a data.table, you must use the `copy()` function. ::: Let's see what happens if we use `copy()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt3 <- copy(dt1) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 75 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79e8253098" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} address(dt3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0x79ea9da000" ``` ::: ::: `dt3` and `dt1` are pointing to different objects in memory, so editing one does not affect the other. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt3[1, HR := 100] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 100 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID GCS HR HR_too 1: 8001 15 75 80 2: 8002 13 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ## Summary | Operation | data.frame | data.table | |--------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------| | `df[["col"]] <- x` | Creates copy | Creates copy | | `dt[, col := x]` | N/A | Modifies in-place | | `df2 <- df1` | df1 unchanged | - | | `dt2 <- dt1` | - | dt1 also changes! | ## Resources - [data.table Reference Semantics](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/data.table/vignettes/datatable-reference-semantics.html)
